expectedText:
EMPLOYEE/APPLICANT SOCIAL MEDIA PASSWORD PROTECTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE
This document describes what California Labor Code § 980 says about an employer's ability to require or request access to an employee's or applicant's personal social media. It is provided for information about Jordan Lee's and Acme, Inc.'s rights and obligations under that statute; it does not itself instruct either party on what to do in any specific situation.

WHAT AN EMPLOYER MAY NOT REQUIRE OR REQUEST
California Labor Code § 980 defines "social media," for purposes of the chapter, broadly — as an electronic service or account, or electronic content, including but not limited to videos, still photographs, blogs, video blogs, podcasts, instant and text messages, email, online services or accounts, or internet website profiles or locations. Using that definition, the statute states that an employer shall not require or request an employee or an applicant for employment to do any of three things: (1) disclose a username or password for the purpose of accessing personal social media; (2) access personal social media in the employer's presence; or (3) divulge any personal social media, except as provided in the statute's own investigation exception. The statute does not distinguish, within this prohibition, between social media content shared publicly and content shared only with a limited audience — the prohibition as written does not turn on that distinction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "As used in this chapter, “social media” means an electronic service or account, or electronic content, including, but not limited to, videos, still photographs, blogs, video blogs, podcasts, instant and text messages, email, online services or accounts, or Internet Web site profiles or locations."
  — California Labor Code § 980(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 980(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=980.)
  "An employer shall not require or request an employee or applicant for employment to do any of the following: (1) Disclose a username or password for the purpose of accessing personal social media. (2) Access personal social media in the presence of the employer. (3) Divulge any personal social media, except as provided in subdivision (c)."
  — California Labor Code § 980(b), Cal. Lab. Code § 980(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=980.)
  Known gap: Both quotations below come from the same single statutory section, Labor Code § 980 — subdivision (a)'s definition and subdivision (b)'s prohibition list — so they are not independent of one another; no second, independently-numbered source was located or used to corroborate this point. This clause describes only what § 980 itself says on its face; it does not address how any court has since construed "personal social media," the presence requirement, or any other term in the statute, and no case law applying § 980 was located or verified in this research. The statute applies by its terms to "an employee or applicant for employment" — this clause does not narrow that to describe obligations toward one and not the other.

EXCEPTION: MISCONDUCT OR LEGAL-VIOLATION INVESTIGATIONS
Labor Code § 980 states one exception to its own prohibition. It does not affect an employer's existing rights and obligations to request that an employee divulge personal social media reasonably believed to be relevant to an investigation of allegations of employee misconduct or of an employee's violation of applicable laws and regulations — provided that the social media disclosed is used solely for the purposes of that investigation or a related proceeding. By its own terms, this exception is tied to an investigation of misconduct or a legal violation, and it conditions use of whatever is divulged to that investigation or a related proceeding; the statute does not state a broader, general-purpose exception beyond that.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Nothing in this section shall affect an employer’s existing rights and obligations to request an employee to divulge personal social media reasonably believed to be relevant to an investigation of allegations of employee misconduct or employee violation of applicable laws and regulations, provided that the social media is used solely for purposes of that investigation or a related proceeding."
  — California Labor Code § 980(c), Cal. Lab. Code § 980(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=980.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes a single subsection, § 980(c), of the same statutory section already cited in the companion clause on the core prohibition — it is not an independent source. The statute states that this exception does not affect the employer's "existing rights and obligations"; it does not itself create a separate, freestanding right to demand social media disclosure — what rights or obligations already exist for a given investigation is a question this clause does not resolve, and no case law construing this exception was located or verified in this research.

EXCEPTION: EMPLOYER-ISSUED DEVICES
Labor Code § 980 states a second exception: nothing in the section precludes an employer from requiring or requesting that an employee disclose a username, password, or other method for the purpose of accessing an employer-issued electronic device. On its face, this exception is limited to accessing the device itself — it addresses employer-issued equipment, not personal social media accessed on that equipment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Nothing in this section precludes an employer from requiring or requesting an employee to disclose a username, password, or other method for the purpose of accessing an employer-issued electronic device."
  — California Labor Code § 980(d), Cal. Lab. Code § 980(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=980.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes a single subsection, § 980(d), of the same statutory section already cited in the companion clauses in this document — it is not an independent source. The statute does not itself define "employer-issued electronic device," and this clause does not attempt to draw the line between that device-access exception and the personal-social-media prohibition in subdivision (b) for a case where personal social media happens to be reachable from employer-issued equipment; no case law on that question was located or verified in this research.

RETALIATION PROTECTION
Labor Code § 980 states that an employer shall not discharge, discipline, threaten to discharge or discipline, or otherwise retaliate against an employee or applicant for not complying with a request or demand by the employer that violates this section. The same sentence states a limit on that protection: the statute does not prohibit an employer from terminating or otherwise taking an adverse action against an employee or applicant if otherwise permitted by law. The statute's own text does not spell out a separate enforcement mechanism, private right of action, or remedy for a violation of this section beyond stating the retaliation prohibition itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer shall not discharge, discipline, threaten to discharge or discipline, or otherwise retaliate against an employee or applicant for not complying with a request or demand by the employer that violates this section. However, this section does not prohibit an employer from terminating or otherwise taking an adverse action against an employee or applicant if otherwise permitted by law."
  — California Labor Code § 980(e), Cal. Lab. Code § 980(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=980.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes a single subsection, § 980(e), of the same statutory section already cited in the companion clauses in this document — it is not an independent source. This research did not locate, within the text of § 980 itself, any provision naming a specific enforcement mechanism, agency, private right of action, or damages/penalty remedy for a violation — that omission is disclosed here rather than filled in with an assumed remedy (for example, an assumption that Labor Code § 98.6, the general retaliation-remedy statute, or the Private Attorneys General Act necessarily applies to a § 980 violation was not checked or verified in this research and is not asserted). What "otherwise permitted by law" means, and how it interacts with the retaliation prohibition in a specific case, is also not resolved by this clause or by any case law verified in this research.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
I, Jordan Lee, acknowledge that I have received and reviewed this description of Labor Code § 980 and Acme, Inc.'s related practices.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
